LOST OR DESTROYED WILL — PRESUMPTION OF REVOCATION AND PROOF — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Pat Morgan · January 15, 2024

PURPOSE OF THIS LOST OR DESTROYED WILL INFORMATION SHEET
This information sheet describes California's statutory and case-law rules that apply when a decedent's original will cannot be located after death, as background in connection with the will of Pat Morgan dated January 15, 2024, following Pat Morgan's death on March 15, 2026, and a petition by Jordan Lee concerning that will. This document covers how a will is revoked by a physical act, the parallel rule for a will executed in duplicate, the statutory presumption that a will last in the testator's possession and missing at death was destroyed with intent to revoke it, the Evidence Code rule defining the effect of that presumption, how the Court of Appeal has described the showing that dispels the presumption and the contestant's burden of proving revocation, and the proof requirements for probating a lost or destroyed will — the petition's written statement of the will's terms, proof of execution by a subscribing witness's affidavit with a photographic copy, and preservation of witness testimony. It does not itself determine whether the will of Pat Morgan was revoked, whether the presumption applies or has been dispelled on any particular facts, or whether any petition satisfies the statutory requirements. This is not a substitute for consulting a licensed attorney about a specific missing will or probate proceeding.

REVOCATION OF A WILL BY A PHYSICAL ACT
California's Probate Code lists the ways a will, or any part of it, is revoked. Apart from revocation by a later will that revokes the earlier one expressly or by inconsistency, a will is revoked by being burned, torn, canceled, obliterated, or destroyed, with the intent and for the purpose of revoking it, by either the testator or another person acting in the testator's presence and by the testator's direction. This is the rule against which a claim that the will of Pat Morgan dated January 15, 2024 was destroyed and thereby revoked is measured: the physical act and the accompanying intent to revoke are both elements of the statute.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-10]
  "Being burned, torn, canceled, obliterated, or destroyed, with the intent and for the purpose of revoking it, by either (1) the testator or (2) another person in the testator’s presence and by the testator’s direction."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 6120(b) (California Legislative Information text), revocation of a will by a physical act done with intent to revoke (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=6120.)
  Known gap: This clause quotes only subdivision (b) of § 6120, the physical-act ground; subdivision (a), revocation by a subsequent will, is not separately quoted. The statute lists the acts and the required intent; it does not itself specify what evidence establishes that a particular act occurred or was accompanied by that intent.

A WILL EXECUTED IN DUPLICATE IS REVOKED BY DESTROYING ONE DUPLICATE
Where a will was executed in duplicate — that is, more than one signed original exists — California law treats the destruction of one duplicate the same as destruction of the will itself. A will executed in duplicate, or any part of it, is revoked if one of the duplicates is burned, torn, canceled, obliterated, or destroyed with the intent and for the purpose of revoking it, by the testator or by another person in the testator's presence and at the testator's direction. The existence of a surviving signed duplicate of the will of Pat Morgan therefore does not, under this section, by itself defeat a revocation accomplished by destroying another duplicate with the required intent.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-10]
  "A will executed in duplicate or any part thereof is revoked if one of the duplicates is burned, torn, canceled, obliterated, or destroyed, with the intent and for the purpose of revoking it, by either (1) the testator or (2) another person in the testator’s presence and by the testator’s direction."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 6121 (California Legislative Information text), revocation of a will executed in duplicate by destruction of one duplicate (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=6121.)
  Known gap: The statute addresses a will "executed in duplicate," meaning multiple signed originals; it does not by its terms address an unsigned photocopy or conformed copy, and it does not itself define how a court determines whether a particular document is a duplicate original as opposed to a copy.

THE STATUTORY PRESUMPTION THAT A MISSING WILL WAS DESTROYED WITH INTENT TO REVOKE
California codifies a presumption of revocation for a missing will. Three conditions trigger it: the testator's will was last in the testator's possession; the testator was competent until death; and neither the will nor a duplicate original of the will can be found after the testator's death. When all three are present, it is presumed that the testator destroyed the will with intent to revoke it. Applied to the will of Pat Morgan dated January 15, 2024, the presumption arises only if each of those three conditions is satisfied — if, for example, the original was last held by someone other than Pat Morgan, or a duplicate original is found after March 15, 2026, the statutory presumption does not arise on its own terms.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-10]
  "If the testator’s will was last in the testator’s possession, the testator was competent until death, and neither the will nor a duplicate original of the will can be found after the testator’s death, it is presumed that the testator destroyed the will with intent to revoke it."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 6124 (California Legislative Information text), the three elements of the presumption that a missing will was destroyed with intent to revoke (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=6124.)
  Known gap: This clause quotes the first sentence of § 6124 (the elements). The second sentence, classifying the presumption as one affecting the burden of producing evidence, is quoted in a separate clause of this document. The statute does not itself define "last in the testator’s possession" or "competent until death" for particular facts.

THE PRESUMPTION AFFECTS ONLY THE BURDEN OF PRODUCING EVIDENCE
The Probate Code classifies the missing-will presumption as a presumption affecting the burden of producing evidence, not the burden of proof. Under the Evidence Code, a presumption of that kind requires the trier of fact to assume the presumed fact — here, that Pat Morgan destroyed the will with intent to revoke it — unless and until evidence is introduced that would support a finding that the presumed fact does not exist. Once such evidence is introduced, the trier of fact determines whether the will was revoked from the evidence itself, without regard to the presumption. The Evidence Code adds that nothing in that rule prevents the drawing of any inference that may otherwise be appropriate from the facts.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-10]
  "This presumption is a presumption affecting the burden of producing evidence."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 6124 (California Legislative Information text), classification of the missing-will presumption as one affecting the burden of producing evidence (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=6124.)
  "The effect of a presumption affecting the burden of producing evidence is to require the trier of fact to assume the existence of the presumed fact unless and until evidence is introduced which would support a finding of its nonexistence, in which case the trier of fact shall determine the existence or nonexistence of the presumed fact from the evidence and without regard to the presumption. Nothing in this section shall be construed to prevent the drawing of any inference that may be appropriate."
  — Cal. Evid. Code § 604 (California Legislative Information text), the effect of a presumption affecting the burden of producing evidence (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=EVID&sectionNum=604.)
  Known gap: Evidence Code § 604 states the general effect of any presumption affecting the burden of producing evidence; it does not itself describe how much or what kind of evidence suffices to dispel the § 6124 presumption in a particular case. The Court of Appeal's description of that showing is addressed in a separate clause of this document.

SUBSTANTIAL EVIDENCE DISPELS THE PRESUMPTION; EQUAL PROBABILITY IS ENOUGH
The Court of Appeal, in Estate of Trikha (2013), described how the § 6124 presumption operates in practice. The court explained that a presumption affecting the burden of producing evidence is not itself evidence but an assumption that aids the trier of fact, and — quoting the earlier decision in Estate of Obernolte (1979), which the court identified as an example of substantial evidence vitiating the common-law revocation presumption later codified in § 6124 — that the effect of the rebuttable presumption of revocation is prima facie only and exists only until rebutted by substantial evidence. The court defined substantial evidence as reasonable and credible evidence of solid value carrying legal significance, which may consist of reasonable and logical inferences drawn from the evidence rather than conjecture or speculation. The Trikha court, again relying on Obernolte, stated that evidence making it equally probable that someone other than the testator destroyed the will satisfies the burden of producing evidence, even though equal probability would not satisfy a burden of proof. In Trikha itself, the court found the presumption overcome by evidence that the decedent had executed the will three weeks before death to carry out a repeatedly expressed wish to provide for all of his children, had never told anyone he intended to revoke it, and that a person who stood to inherit far more under intestacy had both motive and opportunity to take the will.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-10]
  "a presumption affecting the burden of producing evidence is not evidence but merely an assumption designed solely to help the trier of fact reach a determination."
  — Estate of Trikha (2013) 219 Cal.App.4th 791 (California Court of Appeal, Fourth Appellate District, Division Three), a presumption affecting the burden of producing evidence is an assumption aiding the trier of fact, not evidence (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/1040802/estate-of-trikha/)
  "the effect of the rebuttable presumption of revocation of a will is prima facie only; it exists only until rebutted by substantial evidence."
  — Estate of Trikha (2013) 219 Cal.App.4th 791 (California Court of Appeal, Fourth Appellate District, Division Three), quoting Estate of Obernolte (1979) 91 Cal.App.3d 124, the revocation presumption is prima facie only and exists only until rebutted by substantial evidence (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/1040802/estate-of-trikha/)
  "Substantial evidence is defined as reasonable and credible evidence of solid value carrying legal significance."
  — Estate of Trikha (2013) 219 Cal.App.4th 791 (California Court of Appeal, Fourth Appellate District, Division Three), definition of substantial evidence sufficient to overcome the presumption (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/1040802/estate-of-trikha/)
  Known gap: Trikha's discussion of Obernolte and of the specific facts that constituted substantial evidence is summarized in this clause's body; only three of the court's general statements are quoted. The Obernolte opinion itself (91 Cal.App.3d 124) was not independently fetched for this document; its holding is stated here as the Trikha court described it. Whether particular evidence in a specific case rises to the level of substantial evidence is a question the opinion leaves to the facts of each case.

THE CONTESTANT BEARS THE BURDEN OF PROVING REVOCATION
Separate from the burden of producing evidence, the Probate Code allocates the burden of proof at the trial of a will contest. The proponents of the will bear the burden of proof of due execution. The contestants of the will bear the burden of proof of lack of testamentary intent or capacity, undue influence, fraud, duress, mistake, or revocation. In Estate of Trikha (2013), the Court of Appeal applied this allocation to a missing will: the contestant, who alleged the decedent had destroyed his will, had the burden of proving that revocation, while the will's proponent had only the initial burden of producing evidence under § 6124. As applied to the will of Pat Morgan, a party contesting the will on the ground that it was revoked by destruction is the party the statute assigns the burden of proving that revocation.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-10]
  "At the trial, the proponents of the will have the burden of proof of due execution. The contestants of the will have the burden of proof of lack of testamentary intent or capacity, undue influence, fraud, duress, mistake, or revocation."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 8252(a) (California Legislative Information text), allocation of the burdens of proof between proponents and contestants of a will (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=8252.)
  "As a will contestant, Suchitra had the burden of proving Satish revoked his will by destroying it."
  — Estate of Trikha (2013) 219 Cal.App.4th 791 (California Court of Appeal, Fourth Appellate District, Division Three), the contestant alleging destruction of a missing will bears the burden of proving revocation (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/1040802/estate-of-trikha/)
  Known gap: § 8252(a) also provides, in a sentence not quoted here, that when a will is opposed by a petition for probate of a later will revoking the former, the court first determines whether the later will is entitled to probate; and § 8252(b) directs the court to try and determine any contested issue of fact affecting the will's validity. Neither is separately quoted in this clause.

ONCE CONTRARY EVIDENCE IS PRODUCED, THE PRESUMPTION DISAPPEARS AND THE EVIDENCE IS WEIGHED UNDER THE BURDEN OF PROOF
Estate of Trikha (2013) also describes the sequence a court follows. The presumption requires the trier of fact to assume the will was destroyed with intent to revoke unless contrary evidence is introduced; once evidence negating that presumed fact is presented, the presumption drops out and the trier of fact decides the revocation question under the applicable burden of proof, simply by weighing the evidence. In Trikha, the probate court had expressly weighed the evidence and the witnesses' credibility in deciding whether the proponent's evidence was substantial enough to overcome the presumption, principally because it believed the contestant's denial that she destroyed the will. The Court of Appeal held that this was error: by weighing the evidence at that stage, the court engaged in a burden-of-proof analysis in deciding whether the presumption applied, which effectively required the proponent to persuade the court that someone other than the testator destroyed the will — a burden the proponent did not bear. The judgment denying probate was reversed and the matter remanded for a new trial.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-10]
  "Once evidence negating the presumed fact is presented, the trier of fact must decide the case under the applicable burden of proof without regard to the presumption"
  — Estate of Trikha (2013) 219 Cal.App.4th 791 (California Court of Appeal, Fourth Appellate District, Division Three), once contrary evidence is produced, the case is decided under the burden of proof without regard to the presumption (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/1040802/estate-of-trikha/)
  "by weighing the evidence in this fashion, the court erroneously engaged in a burden of proof analysis in determining whether the revocation presumption applied."
  — Estate of Trikha (2013) 219 Cal.App.4th 791 (California Court of Appeal, Fourth Appellate District, Division Three), weighing the evidence in deciding whether the presumption applies is an erroneous burden-of-proof analysis (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/1040802/estate-of-trikha/)
  Known gap: Trikha's holding concerns the distinction between the two burdens and the stage at which evidence may be weighed; it does not decide what the outcome on the merits should be after the presumption disappears, which the opinion left to retrial under the contestant's burden of proof.

THE PETITION FOR PROBATE OF A LOST OR DESTROYED WILL MUST STATE THE TESTAMENTARY WORDS OR THEIR SUBSTANCE
The Probate Code contains a specific pleading requirement for a lost or destroyed will. The petition for probate of such a will must include a written statement of the testamentary words or their substance. If the will is proved, the provisions of the will are set forth in the order admitting the will to probate — so that the order itself, rather than a missing original, records the terms of the will that govern the estate. A petition by Jordan Lee to probate the missing will of Pat Morgan dated January 15, 2024 is therefore subject to this content requirement in addition to the general requirements for any petition for probate.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-10]
  "The petition for probate of a lost or destroyed will shall include a written statement of the testamentary words or their substance. If the will is proved, the provisions of the will shall be set forth in the order admitting the will to probate."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 8223 (California Legislative Information text), required written statement of the testamentary words or their substance, and inclusion of the proved provisions in the order (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=8223.)
  Known gap: § 8223 does not itself specify the form the written statement must take (for example, whether a photocopy of the will attached to the petition satisfies it) or the quantum of proof required to establish the will's provisions; it states only that the petition must contain the statement and that the proved provisions are set out in the order. The general contents of a petition for probate are governed by other sections not addressed in this document.

PROOF OF EXECUTION BY A SUBSCRIBING WITNESS, INCLUDING BY AFFIDAVIT WITH A PHOTOGRAPHIC COPY
Unless the will is contested, California law permits a will to be proved on the evidence of only one of the subscribing witnesses, if that evidence shows the will was executed in all particulars as prescribed by law. The statute also allows evidence of execution to be received by an affidavit of a subscribing witness to which a photographic copy of the will is attached, or by an affidavit in the original will that includes or incorporates the attestation clause. Where the original will of Pat Morgan cannot be found, the provision allowing a subscribing witness's affidavit to be attached to a photographic copy is the mechanism the statute supplies for proving execution from a copy rather than from the original.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-10]
  "The will may be proved on the evidence of one of the subscribing witnesses only, if the evidence shows that the will was executed in all particulars as prescribed by law."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 8220(a) (California Legislative Information text), an uncontested will may be proved on the evidence of one subscribing witness (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=8220.)
  "Evidence of execution of a will may be received by an affidavit of a subscribing witness to which there is attached a photographic copy of the will, or by an affidavit in the original will that includes or incorporates the attestation clause."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 8220(b) (California Legislative Information text), evidence of execution by subscribing-witness affidavit with a photographic copy of the will attached (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=8220.)
  Known gap: These rules apply by their terms only when there is no contest of the will; § 8252(a), addressed in a separate clause, places the burden of proving due execution on the proponents at the trial of a contest. § 8220(c), not quoted here, further permits the court to direct that a subscribing witness's deposition be taken elsewhere, and authorizes examination of the witness on a photographic copy of the will as if the original were present, when no subscribing witness resides in the county.

PRESERVING WITNESS TESTIMONY ABOUT THE WILL'S EXECUTION AND PROVISIONS
Because proof of a lost or destroyed will depends on witnesses to its execution and contents, the Probate Code provides a means of preserving that testimony. The testimony of each witness in a proceeding concerning the execution or provisions of a will, the testamentary capacity of the decedent, and other issues of fact may be reduced to writing, signed by the witness, and filed, whether or not the will is contested. The testimony so preserved, or an official reporter's transcript of it, is admissible in evidence in any subsequent proceeding concerning the will if the witness has become unavailable as a witness within the meaning of Evidence Code § 240. This applies to testimony concerning the will of Pat Morgan whether given in an initial proceeding to prove the will or in a later proceeding.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-10]
  "The testimony of each witness in a proceeding concerning the execution or provisions of a will, the testamentary capacity of the decedent, and other issues of fact, may be reduced to writing, signed by the witness, and filed, whether or not the will is contested. The testimony so preserved, or an official reporter’s transcript of the testimony, is admissible in evidence in any subsequent proceeding concerning the will if the witness has become unavailable as a witness within the meaning of Section 240 of the Evidence Code."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 8224 (California Legislative Information text), reduction of witness testimony to a signed, filed writing and its later admissibility if the witness becomes unavailable (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=8224.)
  Known gap: Evidence Code § 240, which defines when a witness is "unavailable as a witness" for purposes of this rule, is referenced but not separately fetched or quoted in this document.

SIGNATURE AND ACKNOWLEDGMENT BLOCK — LOST OR DESTROYED WILL INFORMATION SHEET

Executed on September 10, 2026 at Oakland, California.

expectedJSON.gap: § 8252(a) also provides, in a sentence not quoted here, that when a will is opposed by a petition for probate of a later will revoking the former, the court first determines whether the later will is entitled to probate; and § 8252(b) directs the court to try and determine any contested issue of fact affecting the will's validity. Neither is separately quoted in this clause.

expectedJSON.body: Estate of Trikha (2013) also describes the sequence a court follows. The presumption requires the trier of fact to assume the will was destroyed with intent to revoke unless contrary evidence is introduced; once evidence negating that presumed fact is presented, the presumption drops out and the trier of fact decides the revocation question under the applicable burden of proof, simply by weighing the evidence. In Trikha, the probate court had expressly weighed the evidence and the witnesses' credibility in deciding whether the proponent's evidence was substantial enough to overcome the presumption, principally because it believed the contestant's denial that she destroyed the will. The Court of Appeal held that this was error: by weighing the evidence at that stage, the court engaged in a burden-of-proof analysis in deciding whether the presumption applied, which effectively required the proponent to persuade the court that someone other than the testator destroyed the will — a burden the proponent did not bear. The judgment denying probate was reversed and the matter remanded for a new trial.

citations.case: Estate of Trikha (2013) 219 Cal.App.4th 791 (California Court of Appeal, Fourth Appellate District, Division Three)
citations.cite: once contrary evidence is produced, the case is decided under the burden of proof without regard to the presumption
citations.quote: Once evidence negating the presumed fact is presented, the trier of fact must decide the case under the applicable burden of proof without regard to the presumption

citations.case: Estate of Trikha (2013) 219 Cal.App.4th 791 (California Court of Appeal, Fourth Appellate District, Division Three)
citations.cite: weighing the evidence in deciding whether the presumption applies is an erroneous burden-of-proof analysis
citations.quote: by weighing the evidence in this fashion, the court erroneously engaged in a burden of proof analysis in determining whether the revocation presumption applied.

expectedJSON.gap: Trikha's holding concerns the distinction between the two burdens and the stage at which evidence may be weighed; it does not decide what the outcome on the merits should be after the presumption disappears, which the opinion left to retrial under the contestant's burden of proof.

expectedJSON.body: The Probate Code contains a specific pleading requirement for a lost or destroyed will. The petition for probate of such a will must include a written statement of the testamentary words or their substance. If the will is proved, the provisions of the will are set forth in the order admitting the will to probate — so that the order itself, rather than a missing original, records the terms of the will that govern the estate. A petition by Jordan Lee to probate the missing will of Pat Morgan dated January 15, 2024 is therefore subject to this content requirement in addition to the general requirements for any petition for probate.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 8223 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: required written statement of the testamentary words or their substance, and inclusion of the proved provisions in the order
citations.quote: The petition for probate of a lost or destroyed will shall include a written statement of the testamentary words or their substance. If the will is proved, the provisions of the will shall be set forth in the order admitting the will to probate.

expectedJSON.gap: § 8223 does not itself specify the form the written statement must take (for example, whether a photocopy of the will attached to the petition satisfies it) or the quantum of proof required to establish the will's provisions; it states only that the petition must contain the statement and that the proved provisions are set out in the order. The general contents of a petition for probate are governed by other sections not addressed in this document.

expectedJSON.body: Unless the will is contested, California law permits a will to be proved on the evidence of only one of the subscribing witnesses, if that evidence shows the will was executed in all particulars as prescribed by law. The statute also allows evidence of execution to be received by an affidavit of a subscribing witness to which a photographic copy of the will is attached, or by an affidavit in the original will that includes or incorporates the attestation clause. Where the original will of Pat Morgan cannot be found, the provision allowing a subscribing witness's affidavit to be attached to a photographic copy is the mechanism the statute supplies for proving execution from a copy rather than from the original.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 8220(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: an uncontested will may be proved on the evidence of one subscribing witness
citations.quote: The will may be proved on the evidence of one of the subscribing witnesses only, if the evidence shows that the will was executed in all particulars as prescribed by law.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 8220(b) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: evidence of execution by subscribing-witness affidavit with a photographic copy of the will attached
citations.quote: Evidence of execution of a will may be received by an affidavit of a subscribing witness to which there is attached a photographic copy of the will, or by an affidavit in the original will that includes or incorporates the attestation clause.

expectedJSON.gap: These rules apply by their terms only when there is no contest of the will; § 8252(a), addressed in a separate clause, places the burden of proving due execution on the proponents at the trial of a contest. § 8220(c), not quoted here, further permits the court to direct that a subscribing witness's deposition be taken elsewhere, and authorizes examination of the witness on a photographic copy of the will as if the original were present, when no subscribing witness resides in the county.

expectedJSON.body: Because proof of a lost or destroyed will depends on witnesses to its execution and contents, the Probate Code provides a means of preserving that testimony. The testimony of each witness in a proceeding concerning the execution or provisions of a will, the testamentary capacity of the decedent, and other issues of fact may be reduced to writing, signed by the witness, and filed, whether or not the will is contested. The testimony so preserved, or an official reporter's transcript of it, is admissible in evidence in any subsequent proceeding concerning the will if the witness has become unavailable as a witness within the meaning of Evidence Code § 240. This applies to testimony concerning the will of Pat Morgan whether given in an initial proceeding to prove the will or in a later proceeding.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 8224 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: reduction of witness testimony to a signed, filed writing and its later admissibility if the witness becomes unavailable
citations.quote: The testimony of each witness in a proceeding concerning the execution or provisions of a will, the testamentary capacity of the decedent, and other issues of fact, may be reduced to writing, signed by the witness, and filed, whether or not the will is contested. The testimony so preserved, or an official reporter’s transcript of the testimony, is admissible in evidence in any subsequent proceeding concerning the will if the witness has become unavailable as a witness within the meaning of Section 240 of the Evidence Code.
